readingInstruction: Read Philemon, a one-chapter letter. It is Paul’s most personal letter, a short appeal on behalf of a runaway slave named Onesimus. Read it slowly, imagining Philemon opening it before the whole church that meets in his house.
settingTheScene: Philemon was a wealthy Christian in Colossae, with a church in his house. His slave Onesimus ran away, perhaps after stealing, and somehow met Paul in prison, where he became a Christian. Paul is sending Onesimus back, with this letter, asking Philemon to receive him not as a slave but as a beloved brother. It was sent with the Colossian letter, carried by Tychicus and Onesimus (Colossians 4:7-9).
observation: “I thank my God always when I remember you in my prayers, because I hear of your love and of the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints” (vv. 4-5).
“For this reason, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do what is required, yet for love’s sake I prefer to appeal to you” (vv. 8-9).
“I appeal to you for my child, Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my imprisonment” (v. 10).
“Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me” (v. 11).
“No longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother” (v. 16).
“So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me” (v. 17).
“If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account” (v. 18).
“Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say” (v. 21).
interpretation:
Paul writes as a prisoner of Christ Jesus, with Timothy, to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church in the house. He begins with thanks for Philemon’s love and faith, and prays that the sharing of his faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing in Christ. Paul has “derived much joy and comfort from your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, my brother.” This builds up goodwill before the request.

Then the appeal. Paul could command, but “for love’s sake I prefer to appeal to you.” The appeal is for Onesimus, whose name means “useful.” Paul puns on it: “Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me.” Paul calls Onesimus his child and says, “I am sending him back to you, sending my very heart.” He would have liked to keep him, but would do nothing without Philemon’s consent, “in order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord.”

Paul offers a perspective on the situation: “For this perhaps is why he was parted from you for a while, that you might have him back forever, no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother.” Providence may have been at work. Onesimus is a brother both in the flesh and in the Lord. Then Paul puts himself in the middle: “So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me. If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it.” He adds, gently, that Philemon owes Paul his very self.

This is a picture of the gospel. Onesimus, the guilty one, owes a debt. Paul, the innocent, steps in and says, charge it to me. Receive him as you would receive me. This is imputation: the debt of the guilty is put on the account of another, and the standing of the innocent is given to the guilty. Christ does this for us before the Father. We are welcomed because we come in his name.

The letter does not directly attack slavery as an institution, though it undermines its foundations by declaring a slave a brother and by asking that he be received as Paul himself. Elsewhere Paul lists slave traders among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10), and the principle that in Christ there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28) worked itself out over time. Paul closes by expressing confidence that Philemon will do even more than he asks, and asks for a guest room, hoping to be released. He sends greetings from Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke.
connection: Colossians 4:7-9 mentions Onesimus. Galatians 3:28 and Colossians 3:11 declare that in Christ there is neither slave nor free. 1 Corinthians 7:21-24 speaks to slaves. Ephesians 6:5-9 gives instruction to slaves and masters. 1 Timothy 6:1-2 mentions believing masters. Isaiah 53:4-6 and 2 Corinthians 5:21 speak of Christ taking our debt. Romans 8:1 assures there is no condemnation. Matthew 18:21-35 teaches forgiveness. Luke 15:20-24 pictures the welcome of the returning son.
application:
Is there someone you need to forgive or receive back? Take a step this week, in the spirit of Paul’s appeal.

Read the letter again, putting yourself in Onesimus’s place, and thank Christ for standing in for you.

Think about whom you may stand beside in an appeal for mercy or justice.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for taking your debt on himself.
Ask him to show you a relationship that needs the grace you have received.
Ask him to help you receive others as brothers and sisters.
